Harold knows that in scenario 2 he felt hopeful and relieved after Arthur’s advice, and he intended to implement the advice by having one-on-one conversations with his team. He also knows that his team members initially appeared open to the idea.

Harold does **not** know in scenario 2 that the strategy will fail. In scenario 3, he comes to know that, despite implementing the advice, the team is still not responding well. This observed lack of improvement is what changes his emotion from hope/relief to disappointment/worry. He does not yet know the specific underlying causes of the team’s problems, such as personal tensions or workload stress; those are only revealed to him later in scenario 4. Arthur’s suggestion about deeper issues comes after Harold is already disappointed and worried.

So the emotion change from scenario 2 to scenario 3 is best explained by the fact that the lack of improvement led to disappointment.
